newsitem.title: UK: Stg bounces off lows but still shaky in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Stg bounces off lows but still shaky in Europe.

text.p: The pound got battered in European morning trading on Friday as dealers took profits and trimmed long positions in the wake of the Labour Party's sweeping victory in the British elections. The pound shed over three pfennigs from pre-election result levels and was down two cents against the dollar. "Sterling has been very strong going into the election, and the big Labour victory will give policy-makers a free hand," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London. "The Labour party has built up a lot of expectations in the markets which it has to live up to now," he said. Dealers said sterling was likely to have a choppy session after being hit by squaring of long positions. "What we are seeing is a wave of profit-taking on a currency that has had a fantastic rally in the past few months," said a senior trader at a German bank. "I still can't see a reversal in trend." At 0750 GMT the pound was at 2.7655/65 marks, down from 2.7970/80 before the election results and from 2.7935/45 at the close here on Thursday. Against the dollar, the pound was at $1.6070/80, down from $1.6253/60 before the results and $1.6236/42 at the European close on Thursday. The Labour party won power for the first time in 18 years in an overwhelming victory. A Labour victory had been expected, but the scale of its majority over the Conservatives took many by surprise. In the 659-seat parliament, Labour won a majority of almost 180, with all but 31 seats counted. Concern that Labour might adopt policies to weaken the strong pound were highlighted by a column in the Times newspaper on Friday, which increased selling pressure in early European trading after a relatively quiet overnight session. The editorialised article said Labour has to adopt policies that will gradually drive down the pound to avoid economic damage to the country and devaluation later. Taxes need to go up so the pressure for interest rates to rise can be eased, the paper said. Selling pressure had mounted on the pound on a misinterpretation of the article as being Labour's position, traders said. "The fact that markets are reacting to this extent to such a story illustrates how much uncertainty there actually is about what kind of policies Labour wants to pursue," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. The prospect of higher British interest rates after the election was the engine fuelling the pound's rally this year, and if fiscal tightening were to reduce the need for higher rates, sterling would be derprived of one of its major attractions, analysts said. Finance minister-in-waiting Gordon Brown moved fast overnight to soothe concerns that he could prove economically lax. "We fully intend to keep all our promises and will move very quickly on a budget," Brown told ITN television news. Brown said a Labour government would deliver the fist budget within two months and would set monetary policy to meet an inflation target of 2.5 percent. "Most will want to see evidence that all pre-election rhetoric and promises will be put into practice," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank America. -- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
